title: Inside the Rainforest
description: Ten standalone texts about tropical forests: the layers from floor to canopy, a night walk in Costa Rica, ants that farm fungus, the Amazon's flying rivers, a plant hunter in Peru, an Indigenous grandmother's knowledge, a ride through the treetops, the soil paradox, a forest under glass in the desert and a forest that went to court.

lessons.title: From Floor to Canopy
lessons.summary: A tour of the four layers of a tropical rain forest, from the dark floor to the giant trees above the canopy.
lessons.text:
Ecologists often classify a tropical rain forest by height, as though it were a building with several floors. The usual scheme has four layers: the forest floor, the dim lower story of shrubs and young trees, the canopy, and the scattered giants that break through it. No living forest respects such neat lines, but the scheme is a useful way to classify what a visitor meets on the climb from the ground to the sky.

The forest floor is darker than most people expect. Only about 2 percent of the sunlight that strikes the top of the forest reaches the ground, and the air there is still, warm and heavy with moisture. Fallen leaves do not pile up for long; they are broken down within weeks. Deer and other browsing animals move quietly through the shade, browsing on the soft shoots of the plants within their reach.

A few yards higher, in the lower story, young trees wait for their chance. Many wait for decades, until an old tree falls and opens a gap of light above them. Their leaves tend to be large and dark, and many have a waxy gloss. The gloss is not mere decoration. It helps the rain run off quickly, so that the leaf dries before mold can settle on it.

The canopy, 100 feet or more above the ground, is where the forest truly lives. Here the crowns of the trees touch and overlap, forming a roof so dense that from an airplane it looks like a calm green sea. Orchids, mosses and other plants that grow on branches without harming the tree adorn almost every surface, and climbing vines adorn the trunks with crimson flowers that seem to hang in the air. Interestingly, many animals of the canopy spend their whole lives here and never touch the ground. Even a reptile may live up here. One thin green snake bears such a close resemblance to a vine that it can hang among real vines and wait, unnoticed, for a lizard to come within reach. That resemblance is its whole strategy, and it is not the only reptile to rely on disguise: many lizards bear a resemblance to bark or to dead leaves.

Above the canopy rise the giants, a few trees that grow 200 feet tall or more. Their crowns stand alone in the full force of the sun and wind, and large eagles build their nests in them. For the scientists who climb them with ropes, the view from the top is breathtaking: a green landscape stretching to the horizon, broken here and there by a crimson or yellow crown in flower. Interestingly, many climbers say that the most breathtaking thing is not the view but the silence.

Questions:
How do ecologists often classify a tropical rain forest?
They classify it by height, in four layers, as though it were a building with several floors.
Why do many leaves in the lower story have a waxy gloss?
The gloss helps the rain run off quickly, so that the leaf dries before mold can settle on it.
How does one green snake catch its food?
Its close resemblance to a vine lets it hang among real vines and wait, unnoticed, for a lizard.
What do climbers see from the top of the giant trees?
The view is breathtaking: a green landscape stretching to the horizon, broken by crowns in flower.

lessons.title: A Night Walk
lessons.summary: A mother and her daughter take a night walk with a guide in Costa Rica and meet frogs, a spider and the tracks of a cougar.
lessons.text:
My daughter, Maya, was nine years old when we took our first night walk in a rain forest, at a small lodge near the eastern coast of Costa Rica. Our guide, Esteban, met us at the start of the trail at seven o'clock. It had been dark for an hour. In the tropics, he explained, the sun does not so much set as switch off.

Before we started, he gave us one rule. "Never put your hand anywhere you have not looked first," he said. "The forest is not dangerous, but it is not kind to careless people." He showed us why within ten minutes. On a branch at the height of Maya's face lay a small yellow snake, coiled and perfectly still. It was a viper, he said, and a careless hand on that branch would have meant a trip to the hospital.

The forest was far louder at night than during the day. Thousands of insects sang at once, and from a pond nearby came a chorus of tiny frogs whose calls sounded exactly like the beep of a microwave oven. Beep, beep, beep, they went, each frog answering another. Then Maya's own watch began to beep, because she had set an alarm for her favorite television program, and Esteban kindly pretended that it was a new species.

At the pond, Esteban lifted a leaf with one finger and showed us a red-eyed tree frog. It was bright green, with blue and yellow sides and enormous red eyes. When the light touched it, its pupils narrowed into thin black slits. Maya was fascinated. She stayed beside the leaf for ten minutes, watching the slits open and close, as fascinated as I had ever seen her. Esteban told her that the frog sleeps by day with its bright colors hidden, and that if a snake disturbs it, the sudden flash of red can confuse the hunter long enough for the frog to escape.

Farther along, a strong, sour odor hung across the trail. "Ew," Maya said, holding her nose. The odor came from peccaries, Esteban said, wild pigs that mark their path with a gland on their backs. A little later, he showed us, in a patch of mud, a track as wide as my palm. It had been made by a cougar. Cougars live in these forests, he said, but they avoid people with great care, and he had seen only three of them in twenty years. Evidently this one had walked here within the past day.

The last animal we met was a large, furry spider sitting at the mouth of its hole. Maya said "ew" again, but she did not step back. Esteban told her that the furry hairs on its body can sense the smallest movement of the air. Evidently she had decided that she liked spiders after all, because on the way back to the lodge, she talked about nothing else.

Questions:
What rule did Esteban give before the walk?
He told them never to put a hand anywhere they had not looked first, because the forest is not kind to careless people.
What happened to the tree frog's pupils when the light touched them?
They narrowed into thin black slits.
Where did the sour odor on the trail come from?
It came from peccaries, wild pigs that mark their path with a gland on their backs.
How often had Esteban seen a cougar?
He had seen only three cougars in twenty years.

lessons.title: The Oldest Farmers
lessons.summary: A professor of plant pathology explains how leafcutter ants grow and protect their fungus gardens.
lessons.text:
Human beings began to farm about 10,000 years ago. By then, leafcutter ants in the forests of Central and South America had already cultivated their crops for millions of years. Lena Ortiz, a professor of plant pathology, the science of plant diseases, has spent her career studying those crops, and she likes to begin her lectures with a simple statement: "These ants are not collecting food. They are collecting fertilizer."

Anyone who has walked through a tropical forest has seen them: a narrow green river of leaf pieces flowing along the ground, each piece held up like a little sail. Every sail has a leaf bearer beneath it, a worker carrying a load several times its own weight. Other workers cut the pieces high in the trees with jaws that work like a pair of garden clippers. The jaws even vibrate as they cut, which helps these living clippers slice through tough leaves.

The ants do not eat the leaves. Inside the nest, smaller workers lick the pieces clean, chew them into a soft paste and plant it with threads of a fungus. This fungus, cultivated by the ants and found almost nowhere else, does what the ants cannot: it carries out the slow degradation of the tough leaf material. In return for this degradation, the ants feed on small swollen tips that the fungus grows for them.

A large colony may contain several million ants, and almost every one of them has a job. The smallest workers act as helpers in an unexpected place: they ride on top of the leaf pieces. These tiny helpers guard each bearer from small flies that try to lay eggs in the bearer's body. When a rich tree is found, the colony can mobilize thousands of workers within minutes, and it can mobilize as many again to repair a flooded tunnel.

Farming, however, brings disease, and here plant pathology becomes important. The ants' gardens can be attacked by a second fungus, a parasite that can destroy a garden in days. To defend it, the ants carry bacteria on their bodies that produce chemicals harmful to the parasite. In effect, the ants use one germ to fight another. They also carry their waste far from the crop, so that no germ can travel from the waste to the food.

The ants have a knack, too, for choosing the right leaves. If a kind of leaf harms the fungus, the workers learn to stop cutting it, even when it looks perfectly healthy. No one fully understands how a colony develops this knack.

Some scientists hope that human farmers might one day emulate these methods: several defenses working together instead of a single chemical, and careful separation of waste. Ortiz doubts that we can fully emulate a system that took millions of years to develop, but she finds it humbling to learn farming from an ant.

Questions:
How do the ants cut leaves?
Their jaws work like garden clippers and even vibrate as they cut.
What does the fungus do that the ants cannot?
It carries out the slow degradation of the tough leaf material.
Why do the smallest helpers ride on the leaf pieces?
They guard each bearer from small flies that try to lay eggs in its body.
How do the ants defend their gardens from disease?
They carry bacteria that fight the parasite, and they keep their waste far from the crop.

lessons.title: Rivers in the Sky
lessons.summary: A climate scientist explains in an interview how the Amazon forest sends rivers of water vapor across South America.
lessons.text:
The phrase "flying rivers" describes the streams of water vapor that the Amazon forest sends into the air and that winds carry across South America. We spoke with Ana Ribeiro, a climate scientist who has studied them for twenty years.

Interviewer: Where does a flying river begin?
Ribeiro: Over the Atlantic. Moist air from the ocean blows west over the forest and drops its rain. The trees pull that water up from the soil and release it through their leaves as vapor, and the air carries it farther west, where it falls as rain again. The same water may fall and rise five or six times before it reaches the Andes.

Interviewer: How much water are we talking about?
Ribeiro: A single large tree can release more than 200 gallons on a hot day. For the whole forest, some estimates suggest around 20 billion tons of water a day, which would be more than the Amazon River itself pours into the ocean. It is a complete reversal of the way we usually picture water. We imagine rivers running downhill to the sea. Here the forest carries the sea inland, against the slope of a continent. People often ask me to explain the reversal twice.

Interviewer: Where does the water go after the Andes?
Ribeiro: The mountains act like a wall. The winds turn south and carry the moisture in a great crescent toward southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina. Much of the rain that waters the farms inside that crescent began its journey in the Amazon.

Interviewer: Why should a farmer far away care about the forest?
Ribeiro: Because his harvest depends on it. When the rainfall drops, crop yields slump, and so does the water behind the dams that produce much of the region's electricity. I find that this idea resonates with farmers more than any chart I could show them. They know what it means to see their income slump in a dry year.

Interviewer: Your work sounds very technical.
Ribeiro: It can be cerebral, yes: satellite data, models, equations. But the cerebral part is only the beginning. In the end, it is about water in a kitchen a thousand miles away.

Interviewer: What threatens the system?
Ribeiro: Clearing the forest. People argue for years about the diversion of a single river for a dam, yet few notice the diversion of the rivers in the sky when the trees are cut. Each new clearing is a setback, and some researchers warn that if too much forest is lost, large areas could slowly turn into dry savanna. That would be a setback no one could undo.

Interviewer: What would you like readers to remember?
Ribeiro: That the market price of forest land is a nominal figure. It measures timber and soil, but not the rain. The nominal price leaves out the most valuable thing the forest does. I hope that message will resonate beyond science.

Questions:
What are flying rivers?
They are streams of water vapor that the Amazon forest sends into the air and that winds carry across South America.
Why does Ribeiro call the flying rivers a reversal?
Because we picture rivers running down to the sea, while here the forest carries the sea inland, against the slope of a continent.
Where do the winds carry the moisture after the Andes?
They carry it in a great crescent toward southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina.
Why does Ribeiro call the market price of forest land a nominal figure?
It measures timber and soil, but not the rain that the forest produces.

lessons.title: The Plant Hunter
lessons.summary: A young biologist joins an eccentric botanist searching the forests of Peru for plants that might become medicines.
lessons.text:
When I applied to join Dr. Ruth Calder's expedition to the forests of eastern Peru, I sent her my vita. It was two pages long and contained very little: a degree, one summer in the field and a short paper about mosses. I later learned that her own vita ran to more than forty pages. She had spent thirty years searching for plants that might become medicines, first on the islands of the Pacific and then in South America.

Her colleagues described her as eccentric, and within a day I understood why. She wore the same faded hat every day, spoke to trees in a low voice as she passed them, and kept a canvas bag slung across her chest, full of notebooks and envelopes. But the eccentric habits concealed a precise and careful mind.

In the evenings, she told me about her early work on kava, a pepper plant grown on islands such as Fiji and Vanuatu. Its root is ground and mixed with water to make a calming drink that people there have shared in ceremonies for centuries. Kava had taught her the lesson she repeated to me most often: the people who live with a plant usually understand it long before scientists do.

Our guide, a man named Julio from a nearby village, proved her right on the second morning. He led us to a thin tree and told us that his grandmother had boiled its bark to treat a sore, dry scalp. Dr. Calder wrote down his words and asked his permission before she touched the tree. Then she cut a small square into the bark to show me the cortex beneath it, a pale, moist layer of living tissue. Many trees, she explained, store their chemical defenses in the cortex, which is why so many medicines have begun as bark. The first effective treatment for malaria came from the bark of a tree that grows on the slopes of the Andes.

Our expedition's medic, Tom, was more skeptical. He reminded us that a remedy for a sore scalp is a long way from a medicine that a pharmacy can sell. Dr. Calder agreed with the medic. She began to fiddle with her hat, as she always did when she was thinking, and said that failure was the normal state of her profession.

Every sample went into a numbered envelope with a note of where it was found and who had told us about it. If a medicine ever came from Julio's knowledge, she said, his village should share in the benefit. Late at night I often watched her fiddle with the envelopes, her bag still slung over one shoulder, checking every label twice.

At the end of the month, she told me that a biologist who expects quick results should study something other than plants. She added that she, too, had once been a young biologist with a two-page vita.

Questions:
Why did her colleagues describe Dr. Calder as eccentric?
She wore the same hat every day, spoke to trees and kept a full canvas bag slung across her chest.
What is kava?
Kava is a pepper plant whose root is made into a calming drink shared in ceremonies on Pacific islands.
What did Julio's grandmother use the bark for?
She boiled it to treat a sore, dry scalp.
Why did Dr. Calder want to see the cortex of the tree?
Many trees store their chemical defenses in the cortex, which is why so many medicines have begun as bark.

lessons.title: The Forest as a Library
lessons.summary: A writer spends a week with an Indigenous grandmother in Ecuador who knows the forest as a scholar knows a library.
lessons.text:
When visitors write about the Indigenous peoples of the Amazon, they often reach for grand words. They speak of a deep communion with nature. Rosa, a grandmother from a small community on a river in eastern Ecuador, laughs at such phrases. When I asked her about communion with nature, she said that what she has with the forest is not communion but study, and that she has been studying it for seventy years.

Rosa is a cheerful, practical woman who speaks quickly and walks faster than I do. On a single morning's walk, she named more than a hundred plants: plants for fevers, palms for roofs, and trees whose fruit draws the animals that her sons hunt. She explained each one with cheerful patience, the way a librarian might explain the arrangement of the shelves.

Her grandson Daniel, who is sixteen, came with us. He is outgoing and loves to talk, and he spends most of the year at a high school in a town, where he studies indoors and plays soccer. In the forest, however, the outgoing boy clammed up. He walked behind his grandmother, listening, and when she asked him the name of a tree, he clammed up again and blushed. Knowledge like hers, Rosa said, is not learned indoors in a single year. It is learned from childhood into adulthood, a little at a time, and Daniel still had all of adulthood ahead of him.

What struck me most was how much of the forest bore the imprint of human hands. Rosa showed me fruit trees growing in what looked like wild forest. Her great-grandparents had planted them in an old garden, and the forest had grown back around them. Researchers have found the same imprint across the Amazon: many forests that look wild were shaped, over centuries, by the people who lived in them.

Rosa's family owns a radio and a boat with a motor, and a tourist once asked her whether such things damaged the authenticity of their culture. Rosa thought the question odd. Her knowledge of the forest, she said, did not lose its authenticity because she used a phone, any more than my knowledge of my city lost its authenticity because I used a map.

On my last day, I asked her what single rule she would bestow on a visitor. She did not offer a commandment from a book. She said only that one should take what one needs and leave the rest, because the forest belongs to the children who have not yet been born. It was the simplest commandment I have ever heard. Before I left, she chose to bestow one more gift on me: a small basket that she had made from palm leaves.

Questions:
How does Rosa describe her relationship with the forest?
She says that it is not communion but study, and that she has been studying the forest for seventy years.
How is Rosa's kind of knowledge learned?
It is learned from childhood into adulthood, a little at a time, and not indoors in a single year.
What did Rosa show the writer about the imprint of human hands?
She showed fruit trees that her great-grandparents had planted in an old garden, around which the forest had grown back.
What rule did Rosa bestow on the visitor?
She said that one should take what one needs and leave the rest, because the forest belongs to the children who have not yet been born.

lessons.title: Above the Trees
lessons.summary: A man who is afraid of heights rides an aerial tram through the canopy in Costa Rica and climbs a viewing tower.
lessons.text:
George had been afraid of heights all his life, so his wife, Helen, was surprised when he agreed to ride the aerial tram on the last day of their vacation in Costa Rica. At seventy-four, he said, it was too late to be afraid of anything.

He dressed for the occasion in his old navy blazer, which he had worn to every family wedding. Helen pointed out that a wool blazer was not ideal for a tropical forest. George replied that if he was going to fall out of the sky, he intended to do it properly dressed.

The tram turned out to be gentle. It was a line of small open cars hanging from a cable, and it moved through the forest no faster than a person walks. The cable carried them slowly up through the trees until they were gliding through the canopy itself, close enough to touch the leaves. George held the rail with both hands for the first ten minutes. By the end of the tram ride, he had let go.

Their guide, Carla, pointed out everything. A toucan sat on a branch a few yards away, using its enormous bill to peck at a cluster of small fruits. It would peck once, pause, and peck again, as if it were choosing the ripest. A group of spider monkeys swung past in a display of gymnastics, leaping between trees with their long arms. George, who had done gymnastics as a boy, said that he had never seen such perfect form.

Then a sound like a great wind rose from somewhere deep in the forest. It was a howler monkey, Carla said, and its roar can be heard more than a mile away. She compared it to a barker outside a circus, calling the whole town to come and see the show. The barker kept calling for several minutes.

After the tram, they climbed a steel tower with a small round platform at the top, shaped like the turret of a castle. Carla set up a telescope on an adjustable stand and lowered it until George could look through it without bending. Helen needed it lower still, and the adjustable stand obliged. From the turret they could see the tops of the tallest trees, with fluffy white clouds resting in the valleys below them. Carla said that the greatest eagle of these forests, the harpy eagle, had become very rare in Costa Rica. Old sailors' tales, she added, spoke of the roc, a bird so large that it carried elephants to its nest. The harpy is no roc, but it can carry off a monkey.

On the way down, George finally took off his blazer and folded it over his arm. He said that the view from the turret, with its fluffy clouds and endless trees, had been worth seventy-four years of fear.

Questions:
Why did George wear his navy blazer?
He said that if he was going to fall out of the sky, he intended to do it properly dressed.
What did the toucan do with its bill?
It used its bill to peck at a cluster of small fruits, as if it were choosing the ripest.
What did Carla compare the howler monkey to?
She compared it to a barker outside a circus, calling the whole town to come and see the show.
What did George and Helen see from the turret?
They saw the tops of the tallest trees and fluffy white clouds resting in the valleys.

lessons.title: The Poor Soil of a Rich Forest
lessons.summary: A soil scientist explains why the richest forest on Earth grows on poor soil, and how ancient people made dark, fertile earth.
lessons.text:
The first time I dug into the soil of the Amazon, I expected something rich and black, the kind of earth that gardeners dream of. What I found, a few inches below the fallen leaves, was a hard clay the deep red of jasper. When I rubbed it between my fingers, it left a fine red grit on my skin. The color comes from iron, the same iron that gives jasper, a stone that people have polished for thousands of years, its warm red glow.

This is the great paradox of the tropical rain forest: the richest forest on Earth grows on some of the poorest soil. Many tropical soils are millions of years old, and the heavy rain has washed most of their nutrients away. In some places the ground is little more than white sand, a pale grit that holds almost nothing.

How, then, does the forest feed itself? It keeps its wealth not in the soil but in its living bodies, and it reuses that wealth with astonishing speed. The forest floor is a kind of graveyard: leaves, branches, insects and animals fall and die there every hour. But it is a graveyard in which nothing stays buried for long. Fungi, bacteria and insects break down a fallen leaf within weeks, while in a northern forest the same leaf might lie for years.

The trees are waiting. Just beneath the leaves lies a thin mat of fine feeder roots, many of them curly and thinner than a thread, wrapped in the threads of helpful fungi. These feeder roots catch the nutrients as soon as they are released, before the rain can wash them away. A piece of this mat lifts like a carpet, its curly roots holding the leaves together from below.

The system is efficient, but it is not flawless. When the forest is cleared and burned, the ash feeds crops for a season or two, and then the rain carries the nutrients off and the harvests fail. A system that is nearly flawless for a forest turns out to be a poor one for a farm.

There is, however, an exception, and it was made by people. Across the Amazon, scientists have found patches of soil so dark and fertile that farmers still dig it up and sell it. It is known as dark earth, and it was created over centuries by Indigenous communities who added charcoal, broken pottery, bones and kitchen waste to the ground near their homes. A farmer near Manaus once filled a barrow with it to show me. It was as dark and soft as a chocolate muffin, and when I broke a handful apart, small pieces of ancient pottery fell out of it like pieces of fruit from a muffin. He pushed the barrow back to the pile and told me that the dark earth stays fertile for centuries.

Questions:
What color was the soil that the writer first dug into?
It was a hard clay the deep red of jasper, because of the iron in it.
What is the great paradox of the tropical rain forest?
The richest forest on Earth grows on some of the poorest soil.
Why does the writer call the forest floor a graveyard?
Leaves, branches, insects and animals fall and die there every hour, but nothing stays buried for long.
How was the dark earth created?
Indigenous communities added charcoal, broken pottery, bones and kitchen waste to the ground over centuries.

lessons.title: A Forest in the Desert
lessons.summary: A curator gives a writer a backstage tour of an indoor rain forest in a desert city, home to a spectacled bear.
lessons.text:
The city stands on the edge of a desert where rain falls on perhaps ten days a year. Yet in its center, under a great dome of glass, there is a tropical forest, with waterfalls and a warm mist that never lifts. The dome was built at the wish of the country's emir, who had visited the Amazon as a young man and wanted the children of his desert to know what a forest feels like.

Maryam, the dome's chief curator, offered to take me backstage, into the parts that visitors never see. Backstage, the forest looks like a factory. Pumps hum behind the rocks, and pipes run under the paths. The rain is real, but it is made by machines. Every drop that falls in the dome is collected, cleaned and stored in an enormous steel vat in the basement, then pumped back to the ceiling to fall again. The vat holds enough water, Maryam said, to fill a large swimming pool.

"People think a rain forest is just trees," she said. "Backstage, you learn that it is mostly water."

The most popular resident of the dome is a bear named Paco. He is a spectacled bear, the only bear of South America, so called because of the pale rings around its eyes that look like glasses. He arrived as a young orphan whose mother had been killed by hunters, and he could not be returned to the wild. Maryam calls him "the old bruin," using an old-fashioned word for a bear, and the old bruin seems to enjoy the attention.

Paco is much smaller than a grizzly. A large male grizzly can weigh twice as much, and while the grizzly eats a great deal of meat and fish, the spectacled bear lives mostly on plants. In the wild, these bears roam the cloud forests of the Andes, climbing trees to reach fruit and building rough platforms of branches to rest on. They feast in particular on the fruit of wild avocado trees, which is much smaller than the avocado sold in a supermarket. Paco cannot roam as far as his wild relatives, but his space is large, with trees to climb.

As we left, a woman was sitting on a bench near the waterfall, quietly beginning to sob. Maryam said that this happened more often than I would think. Many people who work in the city grew up in green, wet countries, and the smell of the dome reminds them of home. Maryam did not see the tears as a failure. A forest that can make a grown woman sob with memory, she said, is doing exactly what the emir hoped a forest would do: it is making people feel something.

Questions:
Why was the dome built?
It was built at the wish of the emir, who wanted the children of his desert to know what a forest feels like.
What happens to the water that falls in the dome?
It is collected, cleaned and stored in a steel vat, then pumped back to the ceiling to fall again.
How is the spectacled bear different from a grizzly?
It is much smaller and lives mostly on plants, while the grizzly eats a great deal of meat and fish.
Why do some visitors sob near the waterfall?
Many of them grew up in green, wet countries, and the smell of the dome reminds them of home.

lessons.title: The Forest in the Courtroom
lessons.summary: A judge decides whether a company may build a golf course on the forested hillside that supplies a town's water.
lessons.text:
The courtroom in San Isidro was small and hot, and on the morning of the ruling every seat was full. Farmers stood along the back wall in their work clothes, and children sat on their parents' knees. The case concerned a forested slope above the town, the source of the stream that gave San Isidro its drinking water.

A development company had bought the land and planned to build a hotel with a golf course on the slope. Its advertisements showed a smiling golfer swinging a club against a background of green mountains. The people of the town pointed out that a golf course in that climate would need water every day, and that the golfer in the picture was standing exactly where their stream began.

Judge Elena Morales, who presided over the case, had a reputation for patience. She had presided over the court for eighteen years and rarely raised her voice. At the start of the hearings, she had told both sides that she saw herself as an umpire, not a player. An umpire, she said, does not care who wins; she cares only that the rules are followed.

The rules, it turned out, had not been followed. Witnesses described how the company's workers had used dynamite to break rock for a road before the permits were approved. After the dynamite, the stream had run brown with mud for weeks. A farmer showed photographs of his cattle refusing to drink.

The company's lawyer was clever and sometimes sarcastic. When an elderly farmer described the forest as the "mother" of the stream, the lawyer asked, in a sarcastic tone, whether the mother also had a lawyer. A few people laughed, but Judge Morales did not. She reminded him quietly that her courtroom was not a theater, and the lawyer apologized.

The town had found support far beyond its farmers. Leaders of churches of every denomination in the region had signed a single letter asking the court to protect the water. Rarely had so many denominations spoken with one voice. Scientists explained that the forest acted like a sponge, holding the rain and releasing it slowly into the stream during the dry season.

On the final morning, Judge Morales read her decision slowly. She said that the region had seen runaway building in recent years, and that runaway building was not the same thing as progress. Then she read the last lines: "The permits for the project are hereby canceled. The company is hereby ordered to repair the road and to plant trees again on the damaged slope."

For a moment, the courtroom was silent. Then the farmers at the back began to clap, and the children clapped because their parents did. Outside, the sky had turned dark, and the first rain of the afternoon was falling on the forest above the town.

Questions:
What was the case about?
It concerned a forested slope above the town, the source of the stream that gave San Isidro its drinking water.
What did the company plan to build?
It planned to build a hotel with a golf course on the slope.
How did Judge Morales describe her role?
She saw herself as an umpire, not a player, who cares only that the rules are followed.
What did the judge order at the end?
She canceled the permits and ordered the company to repair the road and to plant trees again on the damaged slope.
